difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient swap buried in a causal chain. The cardiologist cites a feature that is merely necessary for heart disease to develop and treats it as sufficient to predict the disease.
stimulus: Cardiologist: Every patient who develops coronary artery disease has elevated arterial inflammation at some stage of the disease. Our clinic has begun screening patients' inflammation levels using a new blood panel. Patients whose results show elevated arterial inflammation should therefore be told that they are on track to develop coronary artery disease.
questionStem: The reasoning in the cardiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a screening method whose accuracy has not been independently verified

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that accompanies the development of a disease as if it were enough, by itself, to indicate that the disease will develop

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about individual patients from evidence that concerns only populations

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that arterial inflammation is the underlying cause of coronary artery disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that some patients with coronary artery disease will never be screened at the clinic

explanations.correct: The cardiologist has established only that elevated inflammation is necessary for (accompanies) coronary artery disease. That does not show it is sufficient: plenty of people may have elevated inflammation for other reasons without being on track for heart disease. (B) captures that flaw.
explanations.A: The argument's trouble is logical, not evidentiary — even a perfectly accurate panel wouldn't rescue the inference.
explanations.C: The evidence is already about individual patients ('every patient who develops'), so this misdescribes the stimulus.
explanations.D: A trap: the argument doesn't depend on inflammation being the cause, only on its co-occurrence. The flaw is the sufficiency leap, not an unstated causal claim.
explanations.E: Coverage of the screening program is irrelevant to whether the inference about a screened patient is sound.

difficultyReason: Equivocation on 'free.' The columnist shifts between 'free' meaning 'at no monetary cost' and 'free' meaning 'unconstrained.' The trap choices describe real but adjacent flaws.
stimulus: Columnist: Social-media platforms promise their users a free service, and millions sign up on that basis. But a service whose users are tracked, profiled, and targeted for advertising at every turn is not truly free — the users themselves are the product. So the millions who sign up have been deceived about what they are getting.
questionStem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that advertisers are the only parties who profit from social-media platforms

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on an ambiguity in the meaning of a key term to reach its conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that users who are tracked object to being tracked

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers from the fact that a service has drawbacks that it provides no benefit to its users

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between advertising and tracking for a causal relationship between them

explanations.correct: 'Free' in the platform's promise means 'at no charge'; the columnist shifts to 'free' meaning 'not subject to tracking.' Because the word is used in two senses, the charge of deception doesn't follow.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim advertisers are the sole beneficiaries.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't require users to object — only that they were misled about what 'free' meant.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't deny the service has benefits; it accuses the platforms of misrepresentation.
explanations.E: No causal claim is made; this describes a flaw the argument doesn't commit.

difficultyReason: Cross-population correlation-to-causation slide. A correlation observed in one group (retirees) is imported to explain an outcome in another (working adults). Trap (A) names causation-from-correlation in overly broad form.
stimulus: Economist: In a study of retirees, those who carried high credit-card balances reported significantly higher levels of anxiety than those who were debt-free. The conclusion is obvious: for working adults, paying down credit-card debt is an effective way to reduce anxiety.
questionStem: The reasoning in the economist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from a mere correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from evidence about one population to a claim about a different population without justifying the move

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to specify what counts as a 'high' credit-card balance

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that anxiety is undesirable for working adults

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that retirees and working adults have the same sources of income

explanations.correct: Even granting that debt causes anxiety among retirees, the economist has not shown the same relationship holds for working adults, whose financial lives differ. The move from one population to another is unjustified.
explanations.A: Too broad — and the deeper problem is not the correlation-to-cause move in retirees (which might be fine), but importing that conclusion to a group not studied.
explanations.C: A definitional quibble, not the structural error.
explanations.D: The argument assumes this, but it is common ground; the flaw lies elsewhere.
explanations.E: Too specific — income source is one of many differences, none of which the economist needed to address if the real inference were legitimate.

difficultyReason: Appeal to ignorance disguised as evidence. Absence of evidence for harm is treated as evidence of safety. Trap (C) reverses the actual direction of the flaw.
stimulus: Attorney: The prosecution has produced no document, no witness, and no recording that shows my client was present at the warehouse on the night in question. In the face of such a complete absence of evidence, the jury can only conclude that my client was in fact elsewhere that night.
questionStem: The reasoning in the attorney's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the prosecution's motives instead of the prosecution's evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence for a claim as if it were evidence that the claim is false

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats evidence that a claim is false as if it were evidence that the claim is true

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on a witness whose testimony has not been corroborated

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that any defendant lacking an alibi must be guilty

explanations.correct: The attorney moves from 'no evidence presented that the client was there' to 'the client was elsewhere.' Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence; it is compatible with the client having been there but leaving no trace.
explanations.A: No ad hominem — the attorney critiques the evidence, not the prosecutor.
explanations.C: Reversed: the attorney treats absence of evidence as evidence of a claim, not evidence of falsity as evidence of truth.
explanations.E: The opposite of what the attorney argues.

difficultyReason: Part/whole equivocation — a property of each component is transferred to the collective, though the property is not additive. Trap (A) suggests a sample flaw that is not the move.
stimulus: Architect: Each brick in our new library is, on its own, remarkably lightweight and easy to carry. Our structural engineer confirms this of every brick in the specification. Critics who complain that the library's walls will be too heavy for the old foundation are therefore simply wrong.
questionStem: The reasoning in the architect's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion from evidence about an unrepresentative sample of bricks

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that what is true of each member of a collection must be true of the collection as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on the expertise of an engineer whose credentials are not established

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that some critics may have a financial interest in the library's cancellation

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that the foundation cannot be reinforced

explanations.correct: Each brick is lightweight, but thousands of bricks stacked together produce a weight that is exactly what worries the critics. The architect transfers an individual-level property to the whole.
explanations.A: The engineer confirmed every brick, so representativeness isn't the issue.
explanations.C: The engineer's authority is conceded; the problem is logical.
explanations.D: Ad hominem the architect doesn't actually use; naming it doesn't repair the argument.
explanations.E: Reinforcement could address the concern, but the architect's error is about drawing the 'not too heavy' conclusion in the first place.

difficultyReason: Conditional chain with a necessary/sufficient swap at the end. The conclusion affirms the consequent. Trap (A) sounds right but reverses which direction of the flaw applies.
stimulus: Linguist: If a language has a future tense, then its speakers routinely mark temporal distinctions in their grammar. And speakers who routinely mark temporal distinctions in their grammar develop a habit of precise time reference. Marisol's speakers clearly have a habit of precise time reference. We can therefore conclude that Marisol has a future tense.
questionStem: The reasoning in the linguist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for Marisol's having a future tense as if it were a necessary condition for Marisol's having one

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for Marisol's having a future tense as if it were a sufficient condition for Marisol's having one

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on evidence about the habits of speakers rather than evidence about grammar

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that every language with a future tense uses that tense in the same way

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizes from a single language to a claim about all languages

explanations.correct: The chain establishes: future tense → grammatical time-marking → habit of precise time reference. That makes the habit necessary for (implied by) a future tense, not sufficient for one. The linguist nevertheless concludes the tense from the habit.
explanations.A: Reversed. The habit is established as a necessary condition of having a future tense, not a sufficient one.
explanations.C: The speaker habits are exactly the middle link the argument set up.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't rely on a uniformity claim about future-tense use.
explanations.E: The argument is about Marisol only; no overgeneralization.

difficultyReason: Subtle scope shift between 'species endangered by warming' and 'species for which warming is the chief threat.' Trap (D) names a plausibly related flaw not actually committed.
stimulus: Biologist: Most amphibian species whose habitats have warmed substantially over the past decade are now endangered. It follows that for most endangered amphibian species, habitat warming is the principal threat driving them toward extinction.
questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that habitat warming cannot interact with other environmental threats

choices.label: B
choices.text: shifts from a claim about amphibian species affected by warming to a claim about the causes of endangerment for amphibian species generally

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the past decade from evidence that concerns only recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between two phenomena solely from the fact that they occur together

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that amphibians are representative of all animals threatened by habitat change

explanations.correct: The premise speaks of species whose habitats warmed and are now endangered; the conclusion speaks of endangered species generally and names warming as the chief cause. Endangered amphibian species include many whose habitats have not warmed, and among those whose habitats have warmed, warming may not be the leading threat.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't deny interactions; it just drifts in scope.
explanations.D: A tempting generic flaw, but the argument's deeper trouble is the reference-class shift; the biologist never even fully commits to the pure correlation-to-cause move this answer describes.
explanations.E: No inference from amphibians to other animals is drawn.

difficultyReason: Subtle overgeneralization from 'should, all else equal' to 'should, full stop.' The argument ignores that the principle's ceteris paribus clause may not hold.
stimulus: Ethicist: All else being equal, a person should keep the promises she has made. Mira promised her neighbor that she would water his plants while he was away. It follows that Mira should water her neighbor's plants.
questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a principle that holds only when other considerations are equal and applies it as though no other considerations could be relevant

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes about what people ought to do from a single case

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on the meaning of 'promise' without defining that term

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that neighbors always have a right to expect help from one another

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a description of how people act with a prescription for how they ought to act

explanations.correct: The principle is conditional on all else being equal. Mira might be hospitalized, or the plants might be toxic — conditions under which the promise's force is overridden. The ethicist drops the qualifier in reaching the categorical conclusion.
explanations.B: No generalization — the conclusion is about Mira alone.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't turn on the definition.
explanations.D: Not assumed — the claim is about the promise's force, not a standing right.
explanations.E: Both the premise and conclusion are prescriptive; no is/ought slide occurs.

difficultyReason: Treats an average as if it held of every individual member of the group. Trap (B) names the correct family of error in terms too broad to pin the exact move.
stimulus: Curator: Works by early-career painters in our permanent collection have, on average, appreciated in value more rapidly over the last decade than works by established painters. Donors considering a bequest of a single painting to the museum should therefore expect their gift to appreciate more quickly if the painter is early in her career than if she is established.
questionStem: The reasoning in the curator's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a particular work from evidence about the average performance of a category of works

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats what is true of a group as if it must be true of every member of the group

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on evidence about the last decade to predict performance over a longer period

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that donors may value considerations other than appreciation

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that early-career painters will become established

explanations.correct: A higher average for early-career works does not tell a donor what to expect for any single work. A small number of breakout early-career paintings could lift the average while most individual works underperform established painters.
explanations.B: Too broad — and not quite right. The argument doesn't say every early-career work appreciated faster; it treats the average as if it straightforwardly applied to a particular donor's single painting, which is the sharper description.
explanations.C: The argument does project forward, but the flaw is about averages-vs.-individuals, not time frame.
explanations.D: True but not a reasoning flaw — the conclusion is conditional on caring about appreciation.
explanations.E: Not assumed — the argument compares painters as they stand.

difficultyReason: A self-selected sample is treated as representative. Trap (B) describes an ad hominem attack the argument doesn't make; trap (E) gestures at composition.
stimulus: Policy analyst: A recent survey posted to the city's open-data website asked residents whether the new bicycle-lane network has improved their commutes. More than seventy percent of respondents answered yes. City council can be confident, then, that the bicycle-lane network has improved commutes for most city residents.
questionStem: The reasoning in the policy analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about a population from a group of respondents who may not be representative of that population

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses the views of residents who did not answer the survey by questioning their motives

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a claim about how residents perceive their commutes with a claim about how commutes have actually changed

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that the city council shares the policy analyst's goals

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that because a policy has improved the commutes of individual residents, it has improved the city's commuting patterns overall

explanations.correct: Residents who visit the city's open-data website and fill out a survey about bicycle lanes are disproportionately likely to be cyclists, tech-comfortable, and engaged with the policy — not a cross-section of the city. Their responses don't support a claim about most residents.
explanations.C: Perception/reality is a real gap, but the conclusion is plainly about whether the network has improved commutes, not about a separate objective measure; the sampling flaw is sharper and more clearly fatal.
explanations.D: Not assumed — the conclusion is an empirical claim.
explanations.E: The argument aggregates individuals to a general claim, but the trouble is the respondents' representativeness, not a composition leap from part to whole.
